extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political communication, journalists, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Theory-oriented criteria for understanding how public opinion is formed and distorted by barriers of access, social structures, media practices, language, and time/attention. Useful for analysts evaluating the reliability, reach, and clarity of information flows that shape collective judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to the real environment
rubrics_metrics.description: “Access to the real environment must be limited, before anyone can create a pseudo-environment.” Who actually saw, heard, felt, counted, named the thing about which you have an opinion? Was it the man who told you, or the man who told him, or someone still further removed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask provenance questions — who observed the event, where were they when they watched it, what part of the population did they watch, what newspapers did they read, and who were they permitted to talk to. The distance between event and public opinion is a major source of distortion; tracing directness of access is a protective reminder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and secrecy as information barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Military censorship is 'the simplest form of barrier' but not necessarily the most important because 'it is known to exist, and is therefore in certain measure agreed to and discounted.' Secrecy also includes what is withheld as 'none of the public's business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both overt censorship (e.g., military controls, press service coding) and tacit secrecy or privacy norms (privileged conversations, corporate confidentiality). Known censorship may be discounted by audiences; hidden barriers distort understanding more perniciously. Examples: secret treaties, privileged professional communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy norms and privileged information
rubrics_metrics.description: The frontier between what is concealed for the public interest and what is 'none of the public's business' is elastic: salaries, inheritances, directors' meetings, cabinet meetings, and privileged conversations are commonly treated as private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for culturally and legally varying privacy rules when assessing why certain facts are withheld. Be aware that what a society deems private limits public knowledge and thus shapes opinion indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits upon the circulation of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: There are very distinct limits upon the circulation of ideas; reaching 'everybody' requires extensive machinery, resources, and organization (e.g., Mr. Creel's war-time propaganda apparatus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the scale and resources required to disseminate an idea widely; absent extraordinary effort (war-like mobilization), channels in peacetime are far less inclusive, leaving many enclaves uninformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure and means of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel, trade, mails, wires, radio, railroads, highways, ships, motor cars, and aeroplanes affect the supply and quality of information; technical and economic conditions (passport rules, customs, ports, cables) influence circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess physical and technical access: improvements or restrictions in transport and communications materially change who hears what and how quickly. Monopoly or control of key nodes (cables, ports, terminals) acts as a barrier on exchange of news and opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly, cost, and supply as barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolizing of cables, ports, fuel stations, canals, terminals, market places means more than enrichment — it means a barrier upon the exchange of news and opinion. Cost and available supply can be even greater barriers than monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between deliberate monopolistic control and structural barriers due to cost or insufficient facilities. High costs or inadequate supply produce effective information exclusion even without intentional monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic resources determine access
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a man's income affects his access to the world beyond his neighborhood; with money one can travel, buy books and periodicals, and broaden attention to world facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating who is informed, account for socio-economic differences in the ability to acquire information (travel, subscriptions, leisure). Economic position interacts with cultural preferences to shape information consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-imposed limitations and lack of curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some portions of the public 'suffer from anemia, from lack of appetite and curiosity for the human scene' — they are not barred by external constraints but by habit, leisure choices, and self-indulgence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between structural exclusion and voluntary disengagement. Interventions to improve public knowledge must consider motivational and cultural factors, not only access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social set membership shapes admissible information
rubrics_metrics.description: The social set determines which authors and sources of information are admissible; it fixes canons of Family Tradition, Respectability, Propriety, Dignity, Taste and Form, and administers judgment within its competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze opinion within the context of social sets: what counts as authoritative, who is imitated, and how internal norms validate or exclude information. Social sets act as filters that sort and sanction incoming ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of social leaders and 'radiant points of conventionality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain sets or leaders act as 'radiant points of conventionality' — the socially superior, powerful, successful, rich, and urban sets are likely to be imitated by inferiors; imitation operates vertically and internationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify nodes of influence (elite circles, cosmopolitan sets) that transmit norms and opinions downwards; these act as hubs that can diffuse views widely despite broader fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels between social sets and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal channels from one set to another allow Tarde's laws of imitation to operate; where such channels are absent, mediated portrayals (press, moving pictures) substitute for direct contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing opinion spread, map interpersonal bridges and the extent to which mediated representations versus direct contact form impressions across sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and attention devoted to public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Most people spend little time each day on printed news (estimates around a quarter of an hour among some groups); time available for informing oneself about public affairs is small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure not just access but the scarce time audiences allocate. Short attention spans imply that news must compete strongly for limited daily attention; little time magnifies the effect of selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content preferences shape exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' conscious preferences (local news, politics, finance, editorials, etc.) determine which newspapers or sections they consult; college and business groups showed differing priorities that align with editorial allocations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the match/mismatch between audience preferences and media content. Preferences determine what information people are likely to encounter and thus what forms their opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media space allocation vs public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses (e.g., Wilcox's study) show editors devote a large percentage of space to news and public affairs; historically, editorial allocation corresponded to tastes of certain groups though proportions change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how much editorial space is devoted to public affairs relative to audience demand; both absolute space and proportional shifts matter for information availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and telescoping in news transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: News is often coded, translated, condensed and 'telescoped' (e.g., telegraph coding examples) so that a few words must stand for long successions of acts, thoughts, feelings and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to information loss and distortion introduced by coding, editorial selection, compression for space or transmission cost. Short items may omit context and qualifiers necessary for accurate judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language ambiguity and fluctuating word-meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are 'tokens of value' whose representative meaning 'goes up and down' — national and historical fluctuations change connotations (examples: 'etonnant,' 'awful', and the word-exchange metaphor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for semantic variability across cultures and over time; translators/readers must mentally 'exchange' words across linguistic/cultural currency rates. Failure to adjust leads to inflation or deflation of intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literacy and comprehension limits among audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Millions can scarcely read; many can read but not understand; of those who can both read and understand, only a minority have time to spare. Thus words acquired cue imagined trains of ideas that form opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience literacy and comprehension levels; even grammatically identical messages will produce divergent meanings depending on readers' interpretive resources. Tailor expectations of fidelity accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity: dissociating analogies and attending to differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences and appreciate variety is lucidity of mind — a relative faculty necessary for sound public opinion and not uniformly distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree to which an audience or analyst can discern important distinctions rather than rely on superficial analogies; training and exposure can increase lucidity but it remains a limiting factor in public reasoning.
